quote:
*-ar* verbs take *-e*: *llueva*, *pague*, *insista*.
*-er* and *-ir* verbs take *-a*: *tenga*, *haga*, *ofrezca* (it is *-ca* here).
problem: Two of the three verbs filed under -ar are not -ar verbs, and their forms end in -a, not -e. Llueva is from llover, insista from insistir. Only pague fits. A learner who trusts the rule cannot derive the subjunctive of any verb, and it undoes the vowel flip taught in B1.
authority: Basic Spanish verb morphology: llover is -er, insistir is -ir, pagar is -ar. The script contradicts itself: yourTurn[0].why says llueva has the -a ending of llover, yourTurn[4].why says insistir is an -ir verb that takes -a.
replacement:
*-ar* verbs take *-e*: *pague*, *firme*, *cierre*.
*-er* and *-ir* verbs take *-a*: *llueva*, *insista*, *tenga*, *haga*, *ofrezca*.

quote: With *tú* the verb ends in *-as*: *quieras*, *digas*. With *él*, *ella* or *usted* it ends in *-a*: *quiera*, *diga*.
problem: Stated as a general law but true only of -er and -ir verbs. With -ar verbs the endings are -es and -e: Paga lo que debas is fine, but Vive donde trabajes needs -es. A learner following the rule would write trabajas for trabajes, which is the indicative.
authority: Basic Spanish verb morphology.
replacement: With *tú*, *-er* and *-ir* verbs end in *-as* (*quieras*, *digas*) and *-ar* verbs in *-es* (*pagues*). With *él*, *ella* or *usted*, they end in *-a* (*quiera*, *diga*) and *-e* (*pague*).

quote: They always take the subjunctive.
problem: False for siempre que, one of the four connectors listed. As whenever it takes the indicative, and the course itself teaches that at u17 in g:cuando-indicative (Siempre que llueve, vendemos más tinto), with more in the bank at u46-1303. The learner is told a rule that contradicts a lesson they already passed.
authority: g:cuando-indicative examples[3]; RAE DPD on siempre que is the place to confirm the conditional sense; bank u17-t-cuando-indicative-0028, u46-1303.
replacement: As conditions they take the subjunctive. *Siempre que* can also mean whenever, and then it keeps the ordinary verb, as you already know: *Siempre que llueve, vendemos más tinto.*

quote: *en caso de que*: in case
problem: English in case usually means a precaution taken now, whatever happens. En caso de que means if it should happen. Glossing one as the other leads learners to say Llevo paraguas en caso de que llueva where natives say por si llueve, and to misread notices. It has already produced mismatched bank cards (see the bank claims).
authority: Spanish pedagogical grammars agree: por si + indicative for precaution, en caso de que + subjunctive for a contingency (Yepes, Spanish Grammar Manual; elon.io Latin America course). Butt and Benjamin, ch. on conditional sentences, to confirm.
replacement: *en caso de que*: if, in the event that

quote: With these four phrases, use the wish form, and never *-ría*.
problem: Por si, the native way to say in case, is not taught anywhere. Measured: 0 of 916 scripts contain it, it is not in the graph as a chunk or pattern, and it occurs in 4 of 72,693 bank sentences. An English speaker needs it constantly, and it takes the indicative, which this lesson teaches them to avoid.
authority: Measured with a script across app/content/scripts, graph and bank. Grammar as above.
replacement:
With these four phrases, use the wish form, and never *-ría*.

English *in case* hides two ideas. If you act only when the thing happens, use *en caso de que*: *En caso de que llueva, la reunión es adentro.* If you act now, just to be safe, use *por si* with the ordinary verb: *Llévate un abrigo por si hace frío.* Test: would you do it anyway? Then it is *por si*.

quote:
*a menos que*: unless
*siempre que*: as long as
problem: The rule teaches four connectors and the practice covers two. Examples, Read and Pick and Your Turn contain a menos que 0 times and siempre que 0 times. The 124 targeted bank sentences use a no ser que 54 times, which the rule never mentions, con tal de que 41, en caso de que 29, a menos que 0, siempre que 0. Siempre que as a condition first appears in bank at u59.
authority: Measured with a script over the script file and all bank rows targeting g:subj-conditions.

quote: I'll call you in case there's a problem. (to a friend)
problem: The Spanish means I will call if there is a problem. The English means I will call now as a precaution. Same text at readAndPick[1].options[2] and yourTurn[1].prompt.
authority: As LB2 claim on en caso de que.
replacement: I'll call you if there's a problem. (to a friend)

quote: Cierro con llave en caso de que alguien entre.
problem: Locking up as a precaution is the textbook por si. The Spanish is grammatical, but it reads as a formal contingency, and it is the example that teaches in case. Same sentence at readAndPick[5] and yourTurn[5]. Depends on adding por si to the rule.
authority: Linguist judgement; por si + indicative for precaution in the pedagogical grammars above.
replacement: Cierro con llave por si alguien entra.

quote: a precaution starting with *Llevo… en caso de que…*
problem: The prompt asks for a precaution with the connector that does not express one naturally. Depends on adding por si to the rule.
authority: As above.
replacement: a precaution starting with *Llevo… por si…*

quote:
Put *no* in front and you are no longer vouching, so the verb after *que* switches to the past form that ends in *-ra*: *estaba* becomes *estuviera*, *era* becomes *fuera*, *tenía* becomes *tuviera*, *llegó* becomes *llegara*, *sonó* becomes *sonara*.

*No vi que estuviera enojada.* *No dijo que fuera urgente.* It is the same switch as after *no creo que*.

So does *No es que no quiera, es que no puedo*: the first half is the thing you deny.

English keeps one verb for both. Spanish changes it.
problem: Negation does not force the switch here. Unlike no creo que, these verbs leave a choice, and the choice carries meaning. No vi que estabas ahí says you were there and I missed it. No vi que estuvieras ahí says I saw no sign that you were. No dijo que era urgente says it was urgent and he left that out. The rule erases the distinction and the model the learner needs, and the course already teaches the indicative after no sabía que and no me di cuenta de que.
authority: Mood after negated verbs of perception and communication depends on whether the speaker presupposes the clause: NGLE ch. 25 (modo), Bosque and Demonte 1999 ch. 49, Butt and Benjamin ch. 16 (subjunctive). I could not reach NGLE text during this audit and some learner sources state the flat rule, so the verifier should test with native judgement and CORPES. Internal evidence: u38-0541 No me di cuenta de que estabas aquí, u12-0096 No sabía que venías, ch209 Yo no le dije que hablaba bonito.
replacement:
Put *no* in front and you now have a choice, and it says who is vouching.

Keep the ordinary verb and you still vouch for it: it was true, and someone missed it or left it out. *No vi que estabas ahí.* You were there, and I missed you. *No dijo que era urgente.* It was urgent, and he left that out.

Switch to the *-ra* form and nobody vouches: *estaba* becomes *estuviera*, *era* becomes *fuera*, *tenía* becomes *tuviera*, *llegó* becomes *llegara*. *No dije que fuera urgente.* I never claimed that. *No vi que estuviera enojada.* I saw no sign of it.

With *nadie* or *nada*, use the *-ra* form: *No vi que llegara nadie.* To say you missed something happening, you can also use the plain verb: *No oí sonar el teléfono.*

*No es que* always denies, so it always takes the wish form: *No es que no quiera, es que no puedo.*

English keeps one verb for both. Spanish tells you who stands behind the claim.

quote: No vi que Vale estaba enojada.
problem: Marks correct Spanish as wrong. This is the natural sentence when she was angry and I failed to notice, as in the everyday Perdón, no vi que estabas ahí. The English of the same card, I didn't see that Vale was angry, normally presupposes she was.
authority: Mood after negated verbs of perception and communication depends on whether the speaker presupposes the clause: NGLE ch. 25 (modo), Bosque and Demonte 1999 ch. 49, Butt and Benjamin ch. 16 (subjunctive). I could not reach NGLE text during this audit and some learner sources state the flat rule, so the verifier should test with native judgement and CORPES. Internal evidence: u38-0541 No me di cuenta de que estabas aquí, u12-0096 No sabía que venías, ch209 Yo no le dije que hablaba bonito.
replacement: {"wrong": "No vi que estuvieras ahí. (you know the person was there)", "right": "No vi que estabas ahí.", "why": "You know the person was there, so you still vouch for it: *estabas*. *Estuvieras* would doubt it."}

quote: No dijo que era urgente.
problem: Marks correct Spanish as wrong. It means it was urgent and he did not mention it. A later chapter does exactly this: ch209 Yesid: Yo no le dije que hablaba bonito.
authority: Mood after negated verbs of perception and communication depends on whether the speaker presupposes the clause: NGLE ch. 25 (modo), Bosque and Demonte 1999 ch. 49, Butt and Benjamin ch. 16 (subjunctive). I could not reach NGLE text during this audit and some learner sources state the flat rule, so the verifier should test with native judgement and CORPES. Internal evidence: u38-0541 No me di cuenta de que estabas aquí, u12-0096 No sabía que venías, ch209 Yo no le dije que hablaba bonito.
replacement: {"wrong": "No dijo que era urgente. (you doubt it was urgent at all)", "right": "No dijo que fuera urgente.", "why": "*Era* would mean it was urgent and he left that out. To avoid vouching for it, use *fuera*."}

quote: No vi que Vale estuviera enojada
problem: The checker rejects the indicative for English that most naturally calls for it.
authority: Mood after negated verbs of perception and communication depends on whether the speaker presupposes the clause: NGLE ch. 25 (modo), Bosque and Demonte 1999 ch. 49, Butt and Benjamin ch. 16 (subjunctive). I could not reach NGLE text during this audit and some learner sources state the flat rule, so the verifier should test with native judgement and CORPES. Internal evidence: u38-0541 No me di cuenta de que estabas aquí, u12-0096 No sabía que venías, ch209 Yo no le dije que hablaba bonito.
replacement: ["No vi que Vale estuviera enojada", "No vi que Vale estaba enojada.", "No vi que Vale estaba enojada"]

quote: No dijo que fuera urgente
problem: English He didn't say it was urgent is ambiguous between both Spanish readings, and the indicative is rejected.
authority: Mood after negated verbs of perception and communication depends on whether the speaker presupposes the clause: NGLE ch. 25 (modo), Bosque and Demonte 1999 ch. 49, Butt and Benjamin ch. 16 (subjunctive). I could not reach NGLE text during this audit and some learner sources state the flat rule, so the verifier should test with native judgement and CORPES. Internal evidence: u38-0541 No me di cuenta de que estabas aquí, u12-0096 No sabía que venías, ch209 Yo no le dije que hablaba bonito.
replacement: ["No dijo que fuera urgente", "No dijo que era urgente.", "No dijo que era urgente"]

quote: No oí que sonara el teléfono.
problem: English I didn't hear the phone ring reports missing a real event. Spanish says that with perception verb plus infinitive, taught four days earlier in p:la-vi-salir at u46 d4. Oír que with the -ra form means I did not hear that it rang, leaving open whether it did. Same sentence at readAndPick[4] and yourTurn[3].
authority: p:la-vi-salir; linguist judgement.
replacement: No oí sonar el teléfono.

quote: No oí que sonara el teléfono.
problem: As examples[5]. The natural answer is not accepted.
authority: p:la-vi-salir; linguist judgement.
replacement: {"answer": "No oí sonar el teléfono.", "accept": ["No oí el teléfono.", "No oí que sonara el teléfono.", "No oí que sonó el teléfono."], "why": "You missed something that happened, so *oír* plus the plain verb is the natural choice."}

quote: Tomás no oyó que Vale lo llamara desde la cocina.
problem: Vale did call, so the -ra form casts doubt on a known fact. Natural Spanish uses perception plus infinitive.
authority: p:la-vi-salir; linguist judgement.
replacement: Tomás no oyó a Vale llamarlo desde la cocina.

quote: Vale no oyó que Yesid la llamara.
authority: p:la-vi-salir; linguist judgement.
replacement: Vale no oyó a Yesid llamarla.

quote: No dudo que el proyecto es bueno, pero es muy caro.
problem: Marks correct, indeed the commoner, Spanish as wrong, and directly contradicts g:subj-doubt pitfalls[1], which marks the subjunctive wrong after the same words. A learner is penalised in opposite directions at B1 and B2.
authority: Two lessons contradict each other. Learner references mostly give indicative after no dudo que, while the subjunctive also occurs, especially when conceding, so neither form is wrong. I found no NGLE text on this; check NGLE ch. 25 and DPD dudar.
replacement: {"wrong": "Dudo que el proyecto sea bueno, pero es muy caro.", "right": "No dudo que el proyecto sea bueno, pero es muy caro.", "why": "Almost. *Dudo que* says you think it isn't good. To grant the point first, you need *no dudo que*."}

quote: After *no dudo que* the verb takes its "maybe" form: *sea*.
problem: Presented as a forced choice between sea and es, with es rejected (accept is empty). Both are fine. Accept should include No dudo que el plan es bueno, pero es caro.
authority: Two lessons contradict each other. Learner references mostly give indicative after no dudo que, while the subjunctive also occurs, especially when conceding, so neither form is wrong. I found no NGLE text on this; check NGLE ch. 25 and DPD dudar.
replacement: Both work. *Sea* grants the point for the sake of argument, and *es* says you really are sure. Here you are granting it.

quote: No dudo que tengas razón.
problem: B1 file, flagged because it conflicts with B2. p:concede-pero and nine bank rows at u44 use this construction as correct. Marking it wrong sets up the contradiction.
authority: Two lessons contradict each other. Learner references mostly give indicative after no dudo que, while the subjunctive also occurs, especially when conceding, so neither form is wrong. I found no NGLE text on this; check NGLE ch. 25 and DPD dudar.
replacement: {"wrong": "Dudo que tienes razón.", "right": "Dudo que tengas razón.", "why": "Almost. *Dudo que* takes the wish form. It is *no dudo que* that can keep the plain verb."}

quote: *No dudo que* is certainty, so it takes the indicative.
problem: True as the default, but stated as an absolute that a later lesson breaks.
authority: Two lessons contradict each other. Learner references mostly give indicative after no dudo que, while the subjunctive also occurs, especially when conceding, so neither form is wrong. I found no NGLE text on this; check NGLE ch. 25 and DPD dudar.
replacement: *No dudo que* is certainty, so it usually takes the indicative. Later you will meet it with the subjunctive too, when someone grants a point before a *pero*.

quote: When you retell a conversation after the fact, everything takes one step back, in time and in place. Spanish does it as faithfully as English.
problem: Everything is too strong. If the content still holds, Spanish keeps the tense (Dijo que viene mañana, when tomorrow has not come), and the preterite is often retained, especially in Latin America (Dijo que ya habló con ellos). A learner taught total backshift will mark normal Colombian speech as an error and misjudge what speakers imply.
authority: Backshift in Spanish is not automatic when the content still holds or with a retained preterite: NGLE ch. 24 (tiempos verbales, sequence of tenses), Butt and Benjamin on reported speech. Secondary support: Universidad de Trieste handout on estilo indirecto (Dijo que vendrá hoy a las 5 before 5 pm the next day). NGLE not directly accessed.
replacement: When you retell a conversation after the fact, the verbs usually take one step back, in time and in place, just as in English. Two things can stop that. If what was said still holds right now, you can keep the tense: *Dijo que viene mañana*, if tomorrow has not come yet. And a plain past often stays as it is: *Dijo que ya habló con ellos.*

quote: Vale preguntó dónde está Simón.
problem: Correct Spanish when Simón is still missing. Marked wrong without context, and the why claims the question must step back.
authority: Backshift in Spanish is not automatic when the content still holds or with a retained preterite: NGLE ch. 24 (tiempos verbales, sequence of tenses), Butt and Benjamin on reported speech. Secondary support: Universidad de Trieste handout on estilo indirecto (Dijo que vendrá hoy a las 5 before 5 pm the next day). NGLE not directly accessed.
replacement: {"wrong": "Vale preguntó dónde está Simón. (last week, and he turned up long ago)", "right": "Vale preguntó dónde estaba Simón.", "why": "The question belongs to that past conversation, so it steps back. Keep *está* only if Simón is still missing right now."}

quote: Something that happened before the moment of speaking steps back to *había hablado*.
problem: Presented as a forced choice with hablé rejected (accept is empty), though Hernando dijo que ya habló con ellos is normal, especially in Latin America. Accept should add it.
authority: Backshift in Spanish is not automatic when the content still holds or with a retained preterite: NGLE ch. 24 (tiempos verbales, sequence of tenses), Butt and Benjamin on reported speech. Secondary support: Universidad de Trieste handout on estilo indirecto (Dijo que vendrá hoy a las 5 before 5 pm the next day). NGLE not directly accessed.
replacement: *Había hablado* is the careful choice for something before the moment of speaking. You will also hear *habló*.

quote: A promise about the future steps back to *vendría*, and *mañana* becomes *al día siguiente*.
problem: The rule says vengo becomes venía, and the source line is Mañana vengo, so the rule points to venía. The card asks the learner to pick and rewards vendría, while silently accepting venía.
authority: Internal contradiction between rule and card.
replacement: Both work here. *Venía* steps back from *vengo*, and *vendría* steps back from the future idea. For a promise, *vendría* is clearer. *Mañana* becomes *al día siguiente*.

quote: *aquí* → *allí*
problem: The lesson moves tenses, times and places but not persons, which is where reported speech most often goes wrong: Tengo tu libro must become Dijo que tenía mi libro. It also teaches allí while the examples and Your Turn use the Colombian allá.
authority: Standard treatment of estilo indirecto in any reference grammar.
replacement:
*aquí* → *allí* or *allá*

Who is speaking shifts too. "Tengo tu libro" becomes *Dijo que tenía mi libro*.

quote: Me dijo que me llamará cuando llegue.
problem: Correct Spanish when the arrival is still ahead of the speaker now: He told me he will call when he gets here, and he has not arrived yet. Marked wrong without context.
authority: Backshift in Spanish is not automatic when the content still holds or with a retained preterite: NGLE ch. 24 (tiempos verbales, sequence of tenses), Butt and Benjamin on reported speech. Secondary support: Universidad de Trieste handout on estilo indirecto (Dijo que vendrá hoy a las 5 before 5 pm the next day). NGLE not directly accessed.
replacement: {"wrong": "Me dijo que me llamará cuando llegue. (he arrived last week)", "right": "Me dijo que me llamaría cuando llegara.", "why": "The arrival is already behind you, so both parts step back. If it is still ahead of you now, this sentence is fine."}

quote: Me parece mal que te fueras ayer.
problem: Marks correct Spanish as wrong. A present judgement about a past act is exactly what this sentence says: I think it is wrong that you left yesterday. Present matrix with imperfect subjunctive is standard.
authority: NGLE ch. 24 on correlation of tenses with subjunctive; everyday usage.
replacement: {"wrong": "Me pareció mal que te vas.", "right": "Me pareció mal que te fueras.", "why": "Almost. After *me pareció mal que*, the verb takes the *-ra* form."}

quote: The *-ra* verbs (*fueras, dijeras, avisaran*) follow because the judgement is in the past.
problem: The past of the action alone is enough. The rule implies Me parece mal que te fueras is impossible.
authority: As above.
replacement: The *-ra* verbs (*fueras, dijeras, avisaran*) follow because the judgement or the action is in the past: *Me parece mal que te fueras ayer* works too.

quote: In the past, the next verb is usually in the "-ra" form: *No tenía ni idea de que estuvieras aquí.*
problem: Both forms are natural, and the indicative is at least as common, as with no sabía que. The bank row tagged to this very pattern, u45-0790, uses the indicative: Mi hermana no tenía ni idea de que yo vivía en Bogotá.
authority: Linguist judgement plus evidence from the app itself. NGLE not directly accessible during this audit (rae.es returned 403), so check against NGLE ch. 25 (modo) and CORPES.
replacement: In the past, the next verb can be the ordinary past or the "-ra" form, and both are natural: *No tenía ni idea de que estabas aquí*, *No tenía ni idea de que estuvieras aquí.*

quote: No tenía ni idea de que estás aquí.
problem: The correction implies only the -ra form is possible, and the why says Spanish uses it. Estabas is fine. The sentence with estás is itself acceptable while the person is still here.
authority: Linguist judgement plus evidence from the app itself. NGLE not directly accessible during this audit (rae.es returned 403), so check against NGLE ch. 25 (modo) and CORPES.
replacement: {"wrong": "No tenía ni idea que estabas aquí.", "right": "No tenía ni idea de que estabas aquí.", "why": "Keep the *de* before *que*."}

quote: ¿No crees que sea muy caro?
problem: Grammatical, and common as a more tentative question. It differs in force rather than being an error. The why is fine as far as it goes, but the card presents it as wrong.
authority: Linguist judgement plus evidence from the app itself. NGLE not directly accessible during this audit (rae.es returned 403), so check against NGLE ch. 25 (modo) and CORPES.
replacement: {"wrong": "¿No crees que sea muy caro? (you are sure it is expensive)", "right": "¿No crees que es muy caro?", "why": "You believe it is expensive, so keep the indicative. With *sea* you are really asking, and you lean less hard."}

quote: In the past it is always an ordinary verb: *Mientras estudiaba, trabajaba.*
problem: False for the as long as sense, and the bank proves it at u50-1602: Dijimos que no firmaríamos nada mientras hubiera dudas. See also u50-1610 mientras no tuviera sus cosas.
authority: Bank u50-1602, u50-1610, u50-1588; regular sequence of tenses.
replacement: A past "while" is always an ordinary verb: *Mientras estudiaba, trabajaba.* A past "as long as" takes the *-ra* form: *Dijimos que no firmaríamos nada mientras hubiera dudas.*

quote: Si tuviera plata, habría viajado.
problem: Marked wrong under the claim that both halves need the same time frame. That is false: a lasting condition with a past result is standard (Si fuera más paciente, no habría dicho eso). This sentence is only wrong if the money is about that past moment.
authority: Si + imperfect subjunctive + conditional perfect is a standard mixed conditional when the condition is a standing state: Si fueras más puntual, no te habrías perdido el inicio (todoele teaching material), Si no fuera por ti, me habría muerto. Some UDEP advice lists only the canonical schemas, so check NGLE ch. 47 (condicionales) and Butt and Benjamin ch. on conditional sentences.
replacement: {"wrong": "Si tuviera plata el año pasado, habría viajado.", "right": "Si hubiera tenido plata el año pasado, habría viajado.", "why": "*El año pasado* is over, so the *si* half needs *hubiera tenido*. *Tuviera* only fits what is true now or always, as in *Si fuera más paciente, no habría dicho eso.*"}

quote: Keep the two halves in the same time. A word like *ayer* or *el año pasado* tells you to go to the second pair. You may also mix them on purpose: a past "if" with a result about today, as in *Si hubiera aceptado, hoy viviría en Toronto.*
problem: Only one of the two mixed patterns is allowed. Learners need the other to understand ordinary sentences like Si no fuera tan terco, habría aceptado.
authority: Si + imperfect subjunctive + conditional perfect is a standard mixed conditional when the condition is a standing state: Si fueras más puntual, no te habrías perdido el inicio (todoele teaching material), Si no fuera por ti, me habría muerto. Some UDEP advice lists only the canonical schemas, so check NGLE ch. 47 (condicionales) and Butt and Benjamin ch. on conditional sentences.
replacement: The two halves usually share a time. A word like *ayer* or *el año pasado* tells you to go to the second pair. You can also mix them on purpose. A past "if" with a result about today: *Si hubiera aceptado, hoy viviría en Toronto.* A lasting "if" with a result in the past: *Si fuera más paciente, no habría dicho eso.*

quote: Si supiera, habría venido.
problem: Wrong only in the intended sense of finding out at the time. Si supiera nadar, habría venido is correct. The lesson title promises mixed conditionals and gives only one direction.
authority: Si + imperfect subjunctive + conditional perfect is a standard mixed conditional when the condition is a standing state: Si fueras más puntual, no te habrías perdido el inicio (todoele teaching material), Si no fuera por ti, me habría muerto. Some UDEP advice lists only the canonical schemas, so check NGLE ch. 47 (condicionales) and Butt and Benjamin ch. on conditional sentences.
replacement: {"wrong": "Si supiera, habría venido. (you mean: if I had found out at the time)", "right": "Si hubiera sabido, habría venido.", "why": "*Supiera* is about now or always. For finding out back then you need *hubiera sabido*. *Si supiera nadar, habría venido* is fine, because knowing how to swim is a lasting fact."}

quote: There is no "if" and no "would" here.
problem: The learner met the same form at u29 in g:conditional-past-guess for guessing about the past: tendría veinte años means he was probably twenty. Now La policía tendría pruebas means the police reportedly have evidence. The script never mentions the collision or how to tell them apart.
authority: g:conditional-past-guess rule; RAE Glosario de términos gramaticales lists condicional de conjetura and condicional de rumor separately.
replacement: There is no "if" and no "would" here. Careful: you met this same form for guessing about the past: *Tendría veinte años*, he was probably twenty. A named source or a news report points to the rumour. A story about the past points to the guess.

quote: Write two harmless bits of gossip you have heard about a neighbour or a famous person. Start each one with *según...* and put the verb in the conditional.
problem: The rule says this form lives in news and formal reports, then asks for neighbourhood gossip, where it would sound odd.
authority: Internal contradiction; linguist judgement.
replacement: Write two short news items, in the style of a newspaper, about your town or a famous person. Start each one with *según...* and put the verb in the conditional.

quote: There were reportedly about a hundred people in the square.
problem: By g:conditional-rumour, the simple conditional reports now or later, and a past claim needs habría habido. So reportedly were breaks the rule this pattern requires. With no source and a past reading, Habría unas cien personas is the B1 guess: there must have been about a hundred. Same text at the Read and Pick option.
authority: g:conditional-rumour rule; g:conditional-past-guess rule.
replacement: There are reportedly about a hundred people in the square.

quote: Make it a rumour, "there were reportedly about fifty people": *Había cincuenta personas.*
problem: Rumour of a past fact would be Habría habido unas cincuenta personas under the course's own rule. The answer given, Habría unas cincuenta personas, reports the present.
authority: g:conditional-rumour rule.
replacement: Make it a rumour, "there are reportedly about fifty people": *Hay cincuenta personas.*

quote: They will probably arrive soon.
problem: Llegarán pronto is a plain future. Probably is not in the Spanish, and the conjectural future refers to now, not later (the script itself says Estará en casa is about now). Teaches a wrong link between future tense and probability about the future, and breaks the exact-translation rule.
authority: g:future-conjecture; standard description of the future of probability.
replacement: They will arrive soon.

quote: English says "must have", "will have" or "can have".
problem: The script's own examples use could have. Can have is rare in this meaning.
authority: Examples in the same script.
replacement: English says "must have", "will have" or "could have".

quote: ¿No solo estudias español, sino también trabajas en español?
problem: Sino before a finite verb needs que. This row targets the structure being taught, so the learner is drilled in the error.
authority: DPD sino: when finite clauses are opposed, sino must be followed by que (via search summary, rae.es/dpd/sino returned 403). FundéuRAE recommends no solo..., sino (también). Usage is looser in speech, but formal Spanish and this lesson's register want que.
replacement: ¿No solo estudias español, sino que también trabajas en español?

quote: ¿Tus vecinos no solo hablan mucho, sino también ayudan?
problem: As u44-t-argument-markers-0028.
authority: DPD sino: when finite clauses are opposed, sino must be followed by que (via search summary, rae.es/dpd/sino returned 403). FundéuRAE recommends no solo..., sino (también). Usage is looser in speech, but formal Spanish and this lesson's register want que.
replacement: ¿Tus vecinos no solo hablan mucho, sino que también ayudan?

quote: *No solo… sino también…*: not only this but also that. After a *no solo*, English "but" becomes *sino*.
problem: g:pero-sino promised sino que comes later, and this is where it is needed. Without it, learners extend sino también to finite verbs, as two bank rows do.
authority: DPD sino: when finite clauses are opposed, sino must be followed by que (via search summary, rae.es/dpd/sino returned 403). FundéuRAE recommends no solo..., sino (también). Usage is looser in speech, but formal Spanish and this lesson's register want que.
replacement: *No solo… sino también…*: not only this but also that. After a *no solo*, English "but" becomes *sino*. If a whole new verb follows, add *que*: *No solo vende pan, sino que también enseña a hacerlo.*

quote: English "actually" is not *actualmente* here; use *de hecho*.
problem: Here implies actualmente sometimes means actually. It never does, as p:actualmente says plainly. And correcting someone takes en realidad, not de hecho.
authority: p:actualmente rule; DLE actualmente.
replacement: *Actualmente* never means "actually": it means "nowadays". For "actually", use *de hecho* to add proof and *en realidad* to correct something.

quote: Almost. *En cambio* has no article, and it sits right after the thing you contrast.
problem: Sentence-initial En cambio, nosotros queremos quedarnos is equally correct.
authority: Standard usage of the connector.
replacement: Almost. *En cambio* has no article. It can open the sentence or sit right after the thing you contrast.

quote: *¿Será que…?* is the extra-courteous Colombian opener, followed by *usted* forms.
problem: ¿Será que me puedes ayudar? with tú is ordinary Colombian. g:softening in the same unit says it works with any person. Será que softens, and it does not fix the pronoun. It needs testing with a native Colombian.
authority: Colombian usage, linguist judgement; g:softening yourTurn[6].why.
replacement: *¿Será que…?* is the gentle Colombian opener. It takes *usted* forms here because the request is formal. With a friend it goes with *tú*.

quote: Literally "could it be that you can…". Very Colombian and very courteous.
problem: Placing it above podría as a higher formal rung is doubtful. It is a softener, orthogonal to formality, as ch125 says better: La cuarta es muy bogotana: pides sin pedir.
authority: ch125; linguist judgement.
replacement: Literally "could it be that you can…". Very Colombian: you ask without quite asking.

quote: Almost. *Por favor* does not change the grammar, so a command to a stranger stays blunt.
problem: Misdiagnoses the fault. The real error is tú with señor. Páseme la sal, por favor is perfectly polite, and the same unit teaches Llámeme lo antes posible as a formal command.
authority: p:lo-antes-posible examples[0]; g:commands-usted.
replacement: {"wrong": "Pásame la sal, por favor, señor.", "right": "Páseme la sal, por favor, señor.", "why": "Almost. *Señor* calls for *usted*, so the command is *páseme*. To be gentler still, ask: *¿Me podría pasar la sal?*"}

quote: A command becomes a *podría* question as soon as you say *usted*.
problem: False. Usted has its own commands, taught at A2 and used politely in this unit. Teaches that usted commands are impolite.
authority: g:commands-usted; p:lo-antes-posible.
replacement: To a notary you use *usted*, and a *podría* question is the gentlest way to ask. The plain command would be *Llámeme mañana*.

quote: English softens with "I was wondering…", "could you possibly…" and "I imagine…". Spanish has four matching moves.
problem: Quisiera, the central Spanish softener, is not in this script. 106 of the 120 bank rows targeting g:softening contain it. Measured: only 3 of 916 scripts mention quisiera, all incidentally, none explains it, and no chunk holds it. It first appears in the bank at u40. An unexplained past subjunctive with no trigger undermines everything the learner was told about the subjunctive.
authority: Measured with a script. NGLE 24.2c, via UDEP, on -ra equivalent to the conditional.
replacement:
English softens with "I was wondering…", "could you possibly…" and "I imagine…". Spanish has five matching moves.

*Quisiera* ("I would like") is the politest opener of all. It looks like the past wish form, but here it stands alone with no *que* in front: *Quisiera saber si hay mesa.*

quote: Mariana is writing about the café for her newspaper, and *que* alone sounds too chatty for print. She needs the more careful "who" and "which" that writers use to add a detail about someone.
problem: False claim about register. Rosa, que abrió el café, era la abuela de Tomás is standard in any newspaper. Learners will over-use el cual and sound stilted, which the story itself jokes about in ch155.
authority: Linguist judgement; Butt and Benjamin ch. on relative clauses; ch155 Simón: ¡Lo cual! Vale: Es el único de la casa que habla como usted.
replacement: Mariana is writing about the café for her newspaper. *Que* is still correct in print, but she also wants the more careful "who" and "which" that writers use to add a detail about someone.

quote: With no commas, plain *que* picks out which one.
problem: False after a preposition. El hombre con quien hablé (taught at u33) and la razón por la cual have no commas, and the bank drills this: u48-0006, u48-0016, u48-0060, u48-0068. The true constraint, never stated, is that a bare subject without commas cannot be quien: el vecino quien es doctor is wrong.
authority: g:relatives-prepositions; bank rows cited; Butt and Benjamin ch. on relative clauses.
replacement: With no commas, a plain subject or object takes *que*: *El vecino que es doctor trabaja mucho*, never *El vecino quien es doctor*. After a preposition, *quien* and *el cual* work with no commas: *el hombre con quien hablé*, *la razón por la cual*.

quote: Tomorrow you will meet *lo cual*, for commenting on a whole situation.
problem: The script never says what el cual is for. Its real job is after heavy prepositions and quantifiers, and to mark which noun is meant. The bank has all of this (u48-0012, u48-0041, u48-0064) with no explanation, so the learner meets it as an unexplained pattern.
authority: Bank rows cited; Butt and Benjamin ch. on relative clauses.
replacement:
*El cual* really earns its place after a long preposition (*según la cual*, *a lo largo de la cual*) or a number (*dos de las cuales*), and to show which noun you mean when two are close.

Tomorrow you will meet *lo cual*, for commenting on a whole situation.

quote: La puerta, la cual es muy vieja, no cierra bien.
problem: A subject la cual for a simple description is stilted even in writing. The comic use in ch155 relies on exactly that. Also at rule, readAndPick[3] and yourTurn[2].
authority: Linguist judgement. Butt and Benjamin note que is the norm for simple non-restrictive subjects.
replacement: {"es": "El edificio tiene dos escaleras, una de las cuales está cerrada.", "en": "The building has two staircases, one of which is closed."}

quote: Las mesas, las cuales compró Rosa, son de madera.
problem: As examples[4]. Natural Spanish is Las mesas, que compró Rosa, son de madera. Also at rule and readAndPick[1].
authority: As above.
replacement: {"es": "Hay una grieta por la cual entra agua cuando llueve.", "en": "There is a crack through which water comes in when it rains."}

quote: English drops "whom", but Spanish keeps the preposition: *a quien*.
problem: English cannot drop whom in this clause, and the a is personal a, not a stranded preposition. Your Turn explains it correctly.
authority: yourTurn[1].why in the same script.
replacement: You meet a person, so Spanish needs the personal *a*: *a quien*.

quote: So the recipe is *ser* + the highlight + *quien* / *donde* / *cuando* + the rest.
problem: Omits el que and la que, the commonest spoken form, and the preposition repeat. The bank uses both unexplained: u47-0096 Fue Simón el que dijo, u47-0107 Fue Rosa la que me enseñó, u47-0148 Fue con Vale con quien hablé primero, u47-0146 Es por esto por lo que no firmé. English speakers will write Fue con Vale que hablé.
authority: Bank rows cited; NGLE ch. 40 on copulative relatives to confirm.
replacement: So the recipe is *ser* + the highlight + *quien* / *donde* / *cuando* + the rest. In everyday speech *el que* and *la que* are even more common: *Fue Vale la que encontró la carta.* If the highlight has a preposition, say it twice: *Fue con Vale con quien hablé.*

quote: English does this with stress or "as for". Spanish needs the pronoun: never *El contrato firmé yo.*
problem: A bare noun with no article takes no pronoun. The bank does this at u47-0275: Ni agua nos ofrecieron. Colombian speech uses it all the time: Plata no tengo.
authority: Bank u47-0275; NGLE on topicalisation, to confirm.
replacement: English does this with stress or "as for". Spanish needs the pronoun: never *El contrato firmé yo.* The one exception is a bare noun with no article: *Plata no tengo.*

quote: Conociendo a Don Hernando, va a llegar tarde.
problem: The gerund belongs to the speaker, while the main subject is don Hernando, against the rule in the same script. It works in speech as a speaker comment, but it is a poor model for a lesson on formal compact clauses. Don should be lower case mid-sentence.
authority: RAE on the gerund and its subject; script rule.
replacement: Conociendo a don Hernando, sé que va a llegar tarde.

quote: Never use the gerund for something that happens afterwards.
problem: The commonest gerund error of English speakers, the gerund describing a noun, is warned against nowhere in the course: the man wearing a hat, a box containing letters. Checked here and in g:gerund-ways.
authority: RAE on the gerundio especificativo; Butt and Benjamin ch. on the gerund.
replacement: Never use the gerund for something that happens afterwards. And never use it to describe a noun, the way English does: *the man wearing a hat* is *el hombre que lleva un sombrero*, not *el hombre llevando un sombrero*.

quote: In *Adjunto les envío*, *adjunto* is a verb form: "I attach".
problem: Misanalysis. Envío is the verb, and two finite verbs cannot stand side by side without a link. The DPD describes this invariable adjunto as an adverbial use common in administrative language, so the formula itself is acceptable and must NOT be flagged as an error. The rule's gloss "I attach and send you" repeats the mistake.
authority: DPD adjunto, via search summary (rae.es returned 403) and UDEP Castellano Actual. Verify against the DPD entry.
replacement: In *Adjunto les envío*, *adjunto* works like an adverb, so it never changes: "attached, I send you". With no other verb, as in *Les adjunto mi hoja de vida*, it is the verb *adjuntar*: "I attach".

quote: *Tratarse de* is only used as *se trata de*.
problem: Does not say that it cannot take a subject. English It's about prompts El libro se trata de, which the DPD rejects. It is common in Latin American speech, so the note should be calm.
authority: DPD tratar, via search summary: tratarse de cannot be used with a subject.
replacement: *Tratarse de* is only used as *se trata de*, with no subject in front. For a book or a film, say *El libro trata de la guerra*. You will hear *El libro se trata de la guerra* in speech, but it is not careful Spanish.

quote: For what an object is built from, use *estar fabricado con* plus the material: *está fabricada con madera*.
problem: Taught as the way to say what an object is made of, it pushes learners to Esta mesa está fabricada con madera where anyone says Esta mesa es de madera.
authority: Linguist judgement.
replacement: For what an object is made of, the everyday choice is *ser de*: *La mesa es de madera.* *Estar fabricado con* is the label or catalogue version: *está fabricada con madera*.

quote: When the thing is only possible, or you don't care whether it's true, the verb changes ending: *Aunque llueva, saldré.* In English that is even if.
problem: Omits the subjunctive that grants a known fact and waves it aside. The bank has it, and English even if mistranslates it: u44-0052, u44-0062. Learners cannot understand Aunque seas mi hermano from this rule.
authority: Butt and Benjamin ch. on the subjunctive with aunque; bank rows cited.
replacement: When the thing is only possible, or you don't care whether it's true, the verb changes ending: *Aunque llueva, saldré.* In English that is even if. The same form can admit a known fact and wave it aside: *Aunque seas el dueño, tienes que cumplir la ley.* In English that is "you may be the owner, but".

quote: Even if he's my brother, he's wrong.
problem: He is known to be the brother, so even if is wrong. The Spanish concedes a fact.
authority: Butt and Benjamin ch. on aunque.
replacement: He may be my brother, but he's wrong.

quote: Even if you're the owner, you have to obey the law. (to a man)
authority: Butt and Benjamin ch. on aunque.
replacement: You may be the owner, but you have to obey the law. (to a man)

quote: Aunque llegue tarde, Rosa siempre guardaba una mesa.
problem: Present subjunctive under a past habitual main verb, in a row targeting the structure, with no subject for llegue. The English has someone and arrived, so the two sides do not match either. It is the only such row my scan found in the 14,063 B2 rows.
authority: Sequence of tenses; regex scan of the B2 bank.
replacement: {"es": "Aunque alguien llegara tarde, Rosa siempre guardaba una mesa.", "en": "Even if someone arrived late, Rosa always kept a table."}

quote: To the person in front of you, nothing changes: *Entra*, *no entres*.
problem: False, and the same unit drills the exception: u50-0233 ¡Que bajes ya!, u50-0793 ¡Que te quedes quieto!. Good wishes also go to the listener: u51-0754 Que te vaya muy bien. The lesson title promises wishes, but no example is one.
authority: Bank rows cited; p:que-subj-repeated-order.
replacement: To order the person in front of you, nothing changes: *Entra*, *no entres*. But *que* can go to them in two cases: a good wish (*Que te vaya bien*) and repeating an order that was ignored (*¡Que bajes ya!*).

quote: Tell him I'm not here.
problem: Que le digan means have them tell him. The English gives an order to the listener, the very confusion this lesson removes.
authority: Exact-translation rule; g:que-wishes-commands.
replacement: Have them tell him I'm not here.

quote: The verb after *se* stays singular, whatever follows.
problem: Whatever follows is false: se venden casas, se produjeron dos explosiones, as the course teaches. The singular is right because a clause follows, as pitfalls[1] says correctly.
authority: g:passive-se; pitfalls[1] in the same script.
replacement: The verb stays singular, because a whole *que* clause follows.

quote: *Uno* plus a normal verb: "one" or "you" in general, often including yourself.
problem: A woman speaking of herself can say una. Not stated anywhere in the course. Women also say uno, so this is a note and not a rule.
authority: Linguist judgement; NGLE ch. 16 on indefinite uno, to confirm.
replacement: *Uno* plus a normal verb: "one" or "you" in general, often including yourself. A woman can also say *una*.

quote: The accent marks the stress on *é*, which sounds like *eyes*: *co-MEIS*.
problem: Wrong sound. Spanish éis sounds like English ace. Eyes matches áis. The learner would say co-MICE and confuse it with -áis.
authority: Spanish phonology.
replacement: The accent marks the stress on *é*, and *-éis* rhymes with English *ace*: *co-MEIS*.

quote: Look for the ending *-áis*, *-éis* or *-ís*.
problem: A recognition lesson that misses what learners will read. Hablasteis, hablabais and teníais fit none of these endings, and the bank uses such forms (14 rows in -steis, 7 in -bais or -íais, e.g. u51-0114, u51-0154). Vuestro appears in 0 scripts and 2 bank rows.
authority: Measured with a script.
replacement: Look for the ending *-áis*, *-éis* or *-ís*. Past forms give it away too: *hablasteis*, *comisteis*, *hablabais*, *teníais*. And *vuestro*, *vuestra* mean "your" to a group of friends.

quote: Say it as a friend from Madrid would: Have you all eaten yet?
problem: Your Turn items 0, 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 make the learner type vosotros forms, against the owner's decision of no vosotros in production and the script's own line You will not say these yourself. g:spain-pasts yourTurn 0, 2, 3 and 5 do the same while saying You do not need to produce this. Better: convert Spain forms into Colombian ones, or read and choose.
authority: Standing decision; script rule.

quote: I didn't eat anything today.
problem: Hoy no he comido nada means I haven't eaten anything today, with the day still running, and Colombians say it too, so it does not illustrate a Spain-only habit. The bank has the right English at u51-t-spain-pasts-0024. Same text at readAndPick[1].options[2].
authority: Bank u51-t-spain-pasts-0024; the script's own line about not yet.
replacement: I haven't eaten anything today.

quote: It has a twin ending in *-se*, with exactly the same meaning and uses:
problem: The forms do not alternate when -ra stands for the conditional: polite quisiera, pudiera and debiera cannot become quisiese. The polite-form case is my inference from the general rule.
authority: NGLE 24.2c, via UDEP Castellano Actual: the two endings do not alternate when -ra is equivalent to the conditional.
replacement: It has a twin ending in *-se*, with the same meaning in almost every use (polite *quisiera* is the exception, and stays in *-ra*):

quote: The *-ra* and *-se* forms are two spellings of one tense.
problem: They are two forms, not spellings, and they differ in sound and history. Also at yourTurn[5].why.
authority: Linguist judgement.
replacement: The *-ra* and *-se* forms are two forms of one tense.

quote: Al firmar, se fue.
problem: Marks correct Spanish as wrong, and contradicts the script's own rule that with al the first event can set off the second. The RAE's own example of temporal al + infinitive is Al vernos, se acercó.
authority: RAE, El buen uso del español, el infinitivo, via search summary; the script rule.
replacement: {"wrong": "Al firmar, volvió a Medellín un mes después.", "right": "Tras firmar, volvió a Medellín un mes después.", "why": "Almost. With *al* the two things must touch. With a month between them, use *tras*."}

quote: Llévate un abrigo en caso de que haga frío en la audiencia.
problem: Grammatical, but this is a precaution, where a Colombian says por si. Depends on adding por si to g:subj-conditions. The tagger must retarget this row, because it stops being subjunctive practice.
authority: Pedagogical grammars above; linguist judgement.
replacement: Llévate un abrigo por si hace frío en la audiencia.

quote: Guarda una copia de la carta en caso de que se pierda.
problem: Grammatical, but this is a precaution, where a Colombian says por si. Depends on adding por si to g:subj-conditions. The tagger must retarget this row, because it stops being subjunctive practice.
authority: Pedagogical grammars above; linguist judgement.
replacement: Guarda una copia de la carta por si se pierde.

quote: Compra pan en caso de que venga Hernando.
problem: Grammatical, but this is a precaution, where a Colombian says por si. Depends on adding por si to g:subj-conditions. The tagger must retarget this row, because it stops being subjunctive practice.
authority: Pedagogical grammars above; linguist judgement.
replacement: Compra pan por si viene Hernando.

quote: Lleva el celular en caso de que te necesitemos.
problem: Grammatical, but this is a precaution, where a Colombian says por si. Depends on adding por si to g:subj-conditions. The tagger must retarget this row, because it stops being subjunctive practice.
authority: Pedagogical grammars above; linguist judgement.
replacement: Lleva el celular por si te necesitamos.

quote: Deja la puerta abierta en caso de que llegue alguien.
problem: Grammatical, but this is a precaution, where a Colombian says por si. Depends on adding por si to g:subj-conditions. The tagger must retarget this row, because it stops being subjunctive practice.
authority: Pedagogical grammars above; linguist judgement.
replacement: Deja la puerta abierta por si llega alguien.

quote: Abre la caja en caso de que necesitemos las fotos.
problem: Grammatical, but this is a precaution, where a Colombian says por si. Depends on adding por si to g:subj-conditions. The tagger must retarget this row, because it stops being subjunctive practice.
authority: Pedagogical grammars above; linguist judgement.
replacement: Abre la caja por si necesitamos las fotos.

quote: Llevo los documentos en caso de que los pidan.
problem: Grammatical, but this is a precaution, where a Colombian says por si. Depends on adding por si to g:subj-conditions. The tagger must retarget this row, because it stops being subjunctive practice.
authority: Pedagogical grammars above; linguist judgement.
replacement: Llevo los documentos por si los piden.

quote: Pedimos otro café en caso de que el primero llegue frío.
problem: Grammatical, but this is a precaution, where a Colombian says por si. Depends on adding por si to g:subj-conditions. The tagger must retarget this row, because it stops being subjunctive practice.
authority: Pedagogical grammars above; linguist judgement.
replacement: Pedimos otro café por si el primero llega frío.

quote: Anota el número en caso de que se caiga la llamada.
problem: Grammatical, but this is a precaution, where a Colombian says por si. Depends on adding por si to g:subj-conditions. The tagger must retarget this row, because it stops being subjunctive practice.
authority: Pedagogical grammars above; linguist judgement.
replacement: Anota el número por si se cae la llamada.

quote: Lleva una linterna en caso de que se vaya la luz.
problem: Grammatical, but this is a precaution, where a Colombian says por si. Depends on adding por si to g:subj-conditions. The tagger must retarget this row, because it stops being subjunctive practice.
authority: Pedagogical grammars above; linguist judgement.
replacement: Lleva una linterna por si se va la luz.

quote: I'll let you know in case there's any news.
problem: The Spanish states a condition: this happens only if that does. English in case states a precaution, so the two sides of the card mean different things.
authority: Grammar as in the en caso de que claim; exact-translation rule.
replacement: I'll let you know if there's any news.

quote: In case they don't hear me, raise your hand. (to a friend)
problem: The Spanish states a condition: this happens only if that does. English in case states a precaution, so the two sides of the card mean different things.
authority: Grammar as in the en caso de que claim; exact-translation rule.
replacement: If they don't hear me, raise your hand. (to a friend)

quote: In case Yesid doesn't arrive, I'll start.
problem: The Spanish states a condition: this happens only if that does. English in case states a precaution, so the two sides of the card mean different things.
authority: Grammar as in the en caso de que claim; exact-translation rule.
replacement: If Yesid doesn't arrive, I'll start.

quote: In case there's a problem with the permit, Yesid will sort it out.
problem: The Spanish states a condition: this happens only if that does. English in case states a precaution, so the two sides of the card mean different things.
authority: Grammar as in the en caso de que claim; exact-translation rule.
replacement: If there's a problem with the permit, Yesid will sort it out.

quote: En caso de que Simón escape, cierra la ventana.
problem: The Spanish says close the window if he escapes, which is absurd, since he has gone. The English means close it now so he does not. Rewrite as a precaution.
authority: As above.
replacement: {"es": "Cierra la ventana por si Simón se escapa.", "en": "Close the window in case Simón escapes. (to a friend)"}

quote: Music can be heard in the café since seven.
problem: Ungrammatical English: can be heard does not combine with since.
authority: English grammar; exact-translation rule.
replacement: You've been able to hear music in the café since seven.

quote: Hernando sabe cómo evitar la circulación del centro.
problem: Circulación for traffic reads as Peninsular. The bank elsewhere uses trancón (97 rows) and tráfico (98). All seven u43 rows carry this word to serve l:circulación, marked neutral.
authority: Linguist judgement on Colombian usage; test with a native speaker.
replacement: Hernando sabe cómo evitar el tráfico del centro.

quote: En la próxima primavera, el café cumple cuarenta años.
problem: Bogotá has no spring, so a Bogotá café cannot count time this way. A lexeme forced into the setting. 15 bank rows use primavera or otoño.
authority: Geography; story setting.
replacement: En Toronto, la primavera empieza en marzo.

quote: ¡Lo bonito que está el parque en otoño!
authority: Geography; story setting.
replacement: ¡Lo bonito que está Toronto en otoño!

quote: Por mucho que se queje, Don Hernando vuelve cada mañana.
problem: Don is lower case mid-sentence, as in the other 38 such B2 rows.
authority: RAE, Ortografía 2010: tratamientos in lower case.
replacement: Por mucho que se queje, don Hernando vuelve cada mañana.

quote: Si Don Hernando hubiera manejado esa noche, habría salido un desastre.
problem: Don is lower case mid-sentence, as in the other 38 such B2 rows.
authority: RAE, Ortografía 2010: tratamientos in lower case.
replacement: Si don Hernando hubiera manejado esa noche, habría salido un desastre.

quote: Que Don Hernando venga cada mañana es muy bonito.
problem: Don is lower case mid-sentence, as in the other 38 such B2 rows.
authority: RAE, Ortografía 2010: tratamientos in lower case.
replacement: Que don Hernando venga cada mañana es muy bonito.

quote: Lo tengo clarísimo: no voy a cambiar de opinión.
problem: The chunk being taught never reaches the learner. Session cards show no voy a cambiar de opinión and teach it as meaning I'm absolutely clear on that, a false pairing the learner is then made to type.
authority: Observed in a real session: tools/playtest/render.ts 44 1 and 46 8. Root cause is stripLabel in app/src/exercises/pairs.ts line 44, which treats text before a colon as a label. Fix the code or remove the colon from the content.
replacement: Lo tengo clarísimo. No voy a cambiar de opinión.

quote: I'm absolutely clear on that.
problem: The English covers half of the Spanish, which breaks the exact-translation rule even once the colon is fixed.
authority: Observed in a real session: tools/playtest/render.ts 44 1 and 46 8. Root cause is stripLabel in app/src/exercises/pairs.ts line 44, which treats text before a colon as a label. Fix the code or remove the colon from the content.
replacement: I'm absolutely clear on that. I'm not going to change my mind.
